ahmad-al-mansur.name: Ahmad al-Mansur
ahmad-al-mansur.summary: Saadi Sultan of Morocco from 1578 until his death in 1603, known as al-Dhahabi ('the Golden'), described as a lover of books, calligraphy and mathematics and a connoisseur of mystical texts.

el-badi-palace.name: El Badi Palace
el-badi-palace.summary: A ruined palace in Marrakesh, Morocco, built from 1578 by Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur using materials imported from Italy to Mali to showcase his wealth and power.

riad-architecture.name: Riad
riad-architecture.summary: A garden courtyard divided into four quadrants around a central fountain, historically part of house and palace architecture in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, likely derived from Persian gardens.

sidi-mahrez-mosque.name: Sidi Mahrez Mosque
sidi-mahrez-mosque.summary: Historic mosque in Tunis, Tunisia, also known as Mohamed Bey El Mouradi Mosque, and an official historical monument.

ramadan-muradid-bey.name: Ramadan Bey
ramadan-muradid-bey.summary: Muradid ruler and Bey of Tunis from 1696 until his assassination in 1699, and the youngest son of Murad II Bey.

alawi-dynasty.name: Alawi dynasty
alawi-dynasty.summary: Morocco's ruling royal family since the 17th century, claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad, who ruled as sultans until the 1912 French protectorate and became kings after independence in 1956.

muhammad-iii-of-morocco.name: Muhammad III
muhammad-iii-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1757 to 1790 who rebuilt several cities after the 1755 earthquake, expelled the Portuguese from Mazagan in 1769, and was the first ruler to recognize American independence.

ehzade-mosque.name: Şehzade Mosque
ehzade-mosque.summary: A 16th-century Ottoman imperial mosque in Istanbul, commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent as a memorial to his son Şehzade Mehmed and one of architect Mimar Sinan's earliest major works.

mimar-sinan.name: Mimar Sinan
mimar-sinan.summary: Chief Ottoman architect, engineer and mathematician (c. 1488/1490–1588) under sultans Suleiman the Magnificent, Selim II and Murad III, credited with over 300 structures including the Selimiye Mosque.

court-of-the-lions.name: Court of the Lions
court-of-the-lions.summary: A palace within the Alhambra in Granada, Spain, commissioned by the Nasrid sultan Muhammad V in the late 14th century, famous for its courtyard fountain ringed by twelve sculpted lions.

alhambra.name: Alhambra
alhambra.summary: A palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, begun in 1238 by the first Nasrid emir, with its major palace buildings added in the 14th century and later used as the royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella.

agdal-gardens.name: Agdal Gardens
agdal-gardens.summary: A large historic garden and orchard complex in Marrakesh, Morocco, with old water reservoirs and palaces, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

iznik-pottery.name: Iznik pottery
iznik-pottery.summary: A decorated ceramic ware made in the Anatolian town of İznik from the late 15th to late 17th century, originally inspired by Chinese blue-and-white porcelain but developed into a distinct Ottoman style.

regency-of-algiers.name: Regency of Algiers
regency-of-algiers.summary: A semi-independent Ottoman province on North Africa's Barbary Coast from 1516 to 1830, founded by the Barbarossa corsair brothers and ruled by elected regents who waged naval war on Christian Europe.

ismail-ibn-sharif.name: Moulay Ismail
ismail-ibn-sharif.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1672 to 1727 and second ruler of the 'Alawi dynasty, whose 55-year reign was the longest of any Moroccan sultan, marked by military strength built on a new army including a devoted slave corps, the Black Guard.

tlemcen.name: Tlemcen
tlemcen.summary: The second-largest city in northwestern Algeria, a historic center of the Maghreb blending Arab, Berber, Andalusi, and Ottoman influences.

moulouya-river.name: Moulouya River
moulouya-river.summary: A 520-km river in Morocco running from the Middle Atlas to the Mediterranean, used today for irrigation.

list-of-governors-and-rulers-of-the-rege.name: Dey of Algiers
list-of-governors-and-rulers-of-the-rege.summary: Title for a ruler of the Regency of Algiers, one of several designations—alongside Beylerbey and Pasha—used by its governors.
list-of-governors-and-rulers-of-the-rege.source_title: List of governors and rulers of the Regency of Algiers

battle-of-moulouya.name: Battle of Moulouya
battle-of-moulouya.summary: A May 1692 battle at a river ford in Morocco between the Alawi sultan Moulay Ismail and the Dey of Algiers, ending in Algerian victory.

mustapha-bouchelaghem.name: Mustapha Bouchelaghem
mustapha-bouchelaghem.summary: Bey of the Western Beylik, a region in Algeria, from 1686 to 1734 or 1737, also known as Mustapha Ben Youcef El-Mesrati.

kouloughlis.name: Kouloughlis
kouloughlis.summary: Ottoman-era term for the mixed offspring of Ottoman officials and janissaries with local North African women.

muradid-dynasty.name: Muradid dynasty
muradid-dynasty.summary: Dynasty of beys that ruled Tunisia from 1613 to 1702, succeeded by the Husainid dynasty in 1705.

mascara-algeria.name: Mascara
mascara-algeria.summary: A city in Algeria founded in the 10th century, famous as the hometown of Emir Abd al-Qadir, leader of Algerian resistance to early French colonial rule.

battle-of-jouami-al-ulama.name: Battle of Jouami' al-Ulama
battle-of-jouami-al-ulama.summary: An 1700 battle near Sétif, Algeria, in which Algerian forces defeated the army of the Bey of Tunis, Murad III, forcing his retreat into Tunisian territory.

s-tif.name: Sétif
s-tif.summary: A city in eastern Algeria and Algeria's trade capital, part of ancient Numidia and later the Roman province of Mauretania Sitifensis; site of the 1945 protests and massacre that helped spark the Algerian War.

beylik-of-tunis.name: Beylik of Tunis
beylik-of-tunis.summary: The legal form of present-day Tunisia from 1705 to 1881, ruled by the Husainid dynasty until the French protectorate; it later became a constitutional monarchy after adopting Africa's first constitution.

husainid-dynasty.name: Husainid Dynasty
husainid-dynasty.summary: A Tunisian ruling dynasty of Greek origin from Crete, founded in 1705 by al-Husayn I ibn Ali under Ottoman suzerainty; it ruled Tunisia until the republic's founding in 1957.

al-hasan-al-yusi.name: Al-Hasan al-Yusi
al-hasan-al-yusi.summary: A Moroccan Sufi writer (1631-1691) considered the greatest Moroccan scholar of the seventeenth century, known for his frank autobiographical writing.

saadi-sultanate.name: Saadi dynasty
saadi-sultanate.summary: An Arab Sharifian dynasty that ruled Morocco and parts of Northwest Africa in the 16th and 17th centuries, reaching its height under Ahmad al-Mansur.

ahmad-baba-al-timbukti.name: Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti
ahmad-baba-al-timbukti.summary: Sanhaja Berber writer, scholar and political figure in the western Sudan region who lived from 1556 to 1627 and wrote more than 40 books.

tamegroute.name: Tamegroute
tamegroute.summary: Village near Zagora in Morocco's Draa valley, historically a hub of learning as the center of the Nasiriyya Sufi order, and known for its glazed ceramics.

abu-salim-al-ayyashi.name: Al-Ayyashi
abu-salim-al-ayyashi.summary: Moroccan travel writer, poet, lawyer and Sufi scholar (1628-1679) known for an account of his journeys through the Hejaz.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

abd-al-qadir-al-fasi.name: Abd al-Qadir al-Fasi
abd-al-qadir-al-fasi.summary: A Sufi scholar, living from about 1599 to 1680, who founded the Shadhili zawiyya of Ksar-el-Kebir and was seen as a reviver of Sufism in Fes.

abd-al-rahman-al-fasi.name: Abd al-Rahman al-Fasi
abd-al-rahman-al-fasi.summary: A Moroccan writer on law, history, astronomy and music who lived from about 1631 to 1685 and wrote some 170 books.

shadhili.name: Shadhili
shadhili.summary: A Sufi order founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili in the 13th century, historically influential in the Maghreb and Egypt and followed by millions worldwide.

ksar-el-kebir.name: Ksar el-Kebir
ksar-el-kebir.summary: City in northwestern Morocco whose name means "the big castle," historically home to a Sufi zawiyya and now a major agricultural center.

leo-africanus.name: Leo Africanus
leo-africanus.summary: An Andalusi diplomat and author (c. 1494–c. 1554) best known for his 1526 work on the geography of the Maghreb and Nile Valley, later published as Description of Africa and long considered Europe's most authoritative treatise on the region.

pope-leo-x.name: Pope Leo X
pope-leo-x.summary: Head of the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1513 to 1521, a Medici pope whose sale of indulgences and rejection of Martin Luther's reforms helped spark the Protestant Reformation.

arnoult-de-lisle.name: Arnoult de Lisle
arnoult-de-lisle.summary: French physician, Arabist and diplomat (1556–1613) who married the daughter of a follower of Avicenna in 1586.

coll-ge-de-france.name: Collège de France
coll-ge-de-france.summary: A prestigious higher education and research institution in Paris, founded in 1530 by Francis I of France.

al-rashid-of-morocco.name: Al-Rashid
al-rashid-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1666 to 1672 and the first 'Alawi ruler to unify the country, after conquering Taza, Sijilmasa and Marrakesh.

expulsion-of-the-moriscos.name: Expulsion of the Moriscos
expulsion-of-the-moriscos.summary: A 1609 decree by King Philip III of Spain ordering the removal of Moriscos, descendants of Spain's Muslims forced to convert to Christianity; historians estimate 275,000 to 300,000 were expelled.

aruj-barbarossa.name: Aruj Barbarossa
aruj-barbarossa.summary: Ottoman corsair who became Sultan of Algiers, elder brother of the admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa, and was killed in battle against Spain at Tlemcen.

occhiali.name: Uluj Ali
occhiali.summary: Italian-born privateer (c. 1519–1587) who served as commander of the Regency of Algiers and as Grand Admiral of the Ottoman fleet.

murad-i-bey.name: Murad I Bey
murad-i-bey.summary: First hereditary bey of Tunis (1613–1631) and founder of the Muradid dynasty; born Giacomo Senti in Corsica, he was captured by corsairs as a child and rose through the ranks of the Tunisian court.

pasha.name: Pasha
pasha.summary: A high-rank Ottoman title granted by the Sultan to governors, generals and dignitaries, roughly equivalent to a British Lord; also used in Egypt and Morocco.

al-husayn-i-ibn-ali.name: Al-Husayn I ibn Ali
al-husayn-i-ibn-ali.summary: Founder of the Husainid Dynasty (1675-1740), which ruled Tunisia until the monarchy was abolished in 1957.

ulama.name: Ulama
ulama.summary: Scholars and judges of Islamic doctrine and law, considered guardians, interpreters, and transmitters of religious knowledge, traditionally trained in madrasas.

abdallah-of-morocco.name: Abdallah of Morocco
abdallah-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco who held the throne six separate times between 1729 and 1757, as a son of Sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif.

khalifa.name: Khalifa
khalifa.summary: An Arabic title meaning 'successor,' usually referring to the leader of a caliphate, though it has also been used for other kinds of deputies or viceroys.

ahmad-al-tijani.name: Ahmad al-Tijani
ahmad-al-tijani.summary: Algerian Sufi teacher, born around 1735 to 1737 and died 1815, who founded the Tijaniyyah order after a 1781 vision of Muhammad; it later spread rapidly through North and West Africa.

tijaniyyah.name: Tijaniyyah
tijaniyyah.summary: A Sufi order of Sunni Islam founded by Ahmad al-Tijani after a vision in 1781, originating in Algeria and spreading across the Maghreb and West Africa.

boussemghoun.name: Boussemghoun
boussemghoun.summary: An oasis town in Algeria, home to a Berber-speaking population, where Ahmad al-Tijani founded the Tijaniyyah Sufi order in 1782.

wird.name: Wird
wird.summary: A regular litany and mystical invocation practiced by initiates in Islamic Sufism, repeated as part of devotional discipline.

seven-saints-of-marrakesh.name: Seven Saints of Marrakesh
seven-saints-of-marrakesh.summary: Seven historical Muslim scholars and saints buried in Marrakesh, whose tombs are the focus of a centuries-old annual pilgrimage held over seven days.

essaouira.name: Essaouira
essaouira.summary: A port city on Morocco's Atlantic coast, founded in 1760 by Sultan Mohammed bin Abdallah as a planned hub for foreign merchants; called Mogador until the 1960s, it later became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

khalil-ibn-ishaq-al-jundi.name: Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Jundi
khalil-ibn-ishaq-al-jundi.summary: An Egyptian jurist (died c. 1365) who taught Maliki Islamic law in Medina and Cairo; his legal manual became the most authoritative reference for Maliki law in North and West Africa.

maliki-school.name: Maliki school
maliki-school.summary: One of the four major Sunni Islamic legal schools, founded by Malik ibn Anas in the 8th century, predominant across North and West Africa and parts of the Gulf.

al-qushayri.name: Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri
al-qushayri.summary: An Arab Muslim scholar, theologian and Sufi master born in Nishapur (986–1072), who combined the study of Islamic law and hadith with mysticism and asceticism.

al-risala-al-qushayriyya.name: Al-Risala al-Qushayriyya
al-risala-al-qushayriyya.summary: An 11th-century Arabic manual of Sufism written by al-Qushayri in 1046, defending Sufism as compatible with Sunni Islam and later translated worldwide.

qadiri-order.name: Qadiriyya
qadiri-order.summary: A Sunni Sufi order founded by Abdul Qadir Gilani (1077 to 1166), now widespread across South Asia, China, Turkey, and Africa.

nasiriyya.name: Nasiriyya
nasiriyya.summary: A Sufi order founded by Sidi Mohammed ibn Nasir al-Drawi (1603–1674), centred at Tamegroute in Morocco.

khalwati-order.name: Khalwatiyya (Khalwati order)
khalwati-order.summary: An Islamic Sufi order founded near Herat in medieval Khorasan, widespread today in Egypt, Albania, Bosnia and Turkey, known for strict ascetic and hermitage-based training of its dervishes.

wahhabism.name: Wahhabism
wahhabism.summary: A Salafi revivalist movement within Sunni Islam named after the 18th-century scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, originating in Najd and later spreading across the Arabian Peninsula.

char-bouba-war.name: Char Bouba war
char-bouba-war.summary: A war (1673-1678) in modern Mauritania and Senegal between a Muslim marabout coalition and secular traditional rulers, with lasting effects on the region's society and religion.

morisco.name: Moriscos
morisco.summary: Former Muslims and their descendants in Spain forced to convert to Christianity or face exile; most were expelled between 1609 and 1614, settling largely in Morocco and the Ottoman Empire.

constantine-algeria.name: Constantine
constantine-algeria.summary: Capital of Constantine Province in northeastern Algeria, known as Cirta in Roman times before being renamed after Emperor Constantine the Great; nicknamed the 'City of Bridges'.

kairouan.name: Kairouan
kairouan.summary: City in Tunisia founded by the Umayyads around 670, which became an important center of Sunni Islamic scholarship and Quranic learning.

bizerte.name: Bizerte
bizerte.summary: The capital of Bizerte Governorate in northern Tunisia, the northernmost city in Africa, and the last Tunisian town under French control after independence.

andalusi-arabic.name: Andalusi Arabic
andalusi-arabic.summary: A variety of Arabic spoken from the 8th to 15th century in Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled regions of Iberia, used in administration, literature and poetry until it died out after 1492.

bedouin-arabic.name: Bedouin Arabic
bedouin-arabic.summary: A group of Arabic dialects historically linked to Bedouin tribes, spreading from Najd and the Hejaz since the 10th century across the Arab world.

juan-de-prado.name: Juan de Prado
juan-de-prado.summary: A Spanish Catholic priest who served missions in Muslim Morocco in the 17th century and brought comfort to its small Christian population, before being murdered by the ruler.
